title: Fewest hops is not the fastest route
objective: Learners step through breadth-first search and Dijkstra on the same network and see that the route with the fewest hops (through a satellite relay) is five times slower than a longer chain of fibre links, and how Dijkstra reroutes when a link goes down.

recommended.why: A graph library lays out the network and draws distances, the settled set and the final route straight from the model.

alternative.why: A hand-placed, clickable diagram of the same network tests whether a map-like layout reads better than an automatic one.

assumptions: Latencies are illustrative one-way milliseconds per link, not measurements
Links are symmetric: the same latency in both directions
The satellite relay stands for a geostationary hop of about 260 ms each way
Ties are broken by the order nodes are listed
Timings are playback seconds, 2.5 per step

learnerPrompts.predict: Switch to BFS. It finds a route with fewer hops. Will that route be faster or slower than Dijkstra's, and by roughly how much?
learnerPrompts.explain: Take down the Cairo–Marseille link. Why does Dijkstra's route change while BFS's does not, and why is Frankfurt's distance updated twice?
